title: Living Awake Until the Day Comes
overview: Paul tells a young church that Jesus' return will come without warning, so they should live alert and kind toward each other, and he closes with short instructions and a blessing.

parts.label: Like a thief at night (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The "day of the Lord" here means the time Jesus returns and God judges the world, and Paul says nobody can name the date: it will come as unexpectedly as a burglar. Like labor pains, it will arrive suddenly and cannot be stopped, even while people feel calm and secure.

parts.label: People of the day (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: Night stands for careless, unaware living and day for living openly and alert, and Paul pictures faith, love and hope as a soldier's chest armor and helmet. Whether believers are still alive or have died ("asleep") when Jesus comes, they will be with him together, so they should keep encouraging each other.

parts.label: Caring for the community (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Paul asks them to respect the leaders who work hard guiding and correcting them, keep the peace, and never pay back wrong for wrong. The "idle" were probably people who had stopped working and were living off others, possibly because they expected Jesus back very soon, though scholars are not certain of the reason.

parts.label: Short rules for daily life (vv. 16-22)
parts.note: Paul gives quick instructions: be glad, keep praying, and give thanks whatever happens. Not quenching the Spirit means not smothering God's work among them, including messages people spoke as if from God, which they should weigh, keeping what is good and refusing what is evil.

parts.label: Blessing and goodbyes (vv. 23-28)
parts.note: Paul prays that God would make them whole and good in every part of who they are, and says God can be trusted to do it. The "holy kiss" was a warm greeting early churches used as a sign of belonging, and Paul solemnly insists that the letter be read to every member, though he does not say why.

disagreement: Christians differ on how this chapter fits into a wider timeline of the end, for example whether God's promise not to appoint believers to wrath (v. 9) means they will be taken away before a final time of trouble or kept safe through it.
think: If you knew a big change was coming but not when, how might that shape the way you treat the people around you now?
